access.edition_or_version: Sanskrit original c. 4th-5th century CE (date left null rather than asserted); A. W. Ryder translation in Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works, J. M. Dent (Everyman's Library), London, 1912 (some catalogues 1914); about 111-119 verses by recension, commonly cited as 111

mechanics.premise: A yaksha, exiled from his beloved wife by his lord's curse, asks a passing monsoon cloud to carry his message to her; the cloud's route across the subcontinent is described by landmarks and seasons while separation-longing saturates each stage.
mechanics.point_of_view: Third-person frame around first-person-voiced pleas from the yaksha to the cloud, with the wife addressed inside the carried message.
mechanics.psychic_distance: Alternates between intimate address to the cloud and the absent wife and wide landscape panoramas - scale shifts do the emotional work.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Elaborate Sanskrit kavya ornament; a sustained metaphoric chain (cloud as courier, journey as emotion); catalogues of place and season; landscape description doubling as emotional sequence.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Appeal - outward journey widening the world - message of remembered intimacy - anticipation of reunion; distance increases while feeling intensifies.
mechanics.dialogue: Sustained apostrophe: the yaksha speaks to the cloud throughout, the beloved heard within the message he sends.
mechanics.conventions: Classical sandha-kavya (message poem); separation-longing is a common theme in Sanskrit love poetry.
mechanics.innovation_or_subversion: Turns the physical journey of the messenger into the structure of longing itself - affect carried across geography rather than narrated as private interiority.
mechanics.critical_reception: Among the most celebrated Sanskrit poems; translated many times, Ryder's Cloud-Messenger among the standard English versions.
mechanics.audience_reception: Traditional fame tied to its landscape catalogues; recited and anthologized across centuries.
